title: Complexity Analysis + STL
tagline: learn to COUNT work before writing a single line

placementQuiz.q: A loop runs n times and inside it another loop runs n times. Total passes?
placementQuiz.explain: Nested loops multiply: each of the n outer passes does n inner passes.

placementQuiz.q: Two loops placed one after another, each running n times. Total?
Searching one item in an unsorted list of n things needs, in the worst day…
options: look at every one of them
placementQuiz.explain: Unlucky case: it's the last item or missing — full scan.

placementQuiz.q: Which keeps items SORTED automatically after every insert?
placementQuiz.explain: set refuses duplicates and files everything in order.

placementQuiz.q: `v.push_back(5)` on a vector adds the value…

blocks.md: Every program is a machine **moving through steps**. Before trusting code, ask: *how many moves does this make as my data grows?* Two programs giving the same answer can differ by MILLIONS of moves — the fast one feels instant, the slow one freezes.
**Count the passes over your data — that number decides whether your program finishes or freezes.**

steps: Look at the input size (call it n)
Find every loop and ask how many times it runs
Loops stacked INSIDE each other multiply their counts
Loops sitting AFTER each other add their counts

items.q: Printing every element of a list of 1000 items takes how many print-moves?
items.explain: One pass = one move per item.

items.q: Checking every PAIR in a 1000-item list (each with each) is closest to…
items.explain: 1000 × 1000 = a million. Pairs explode — remember this feeling.

items: **One pass** over n items → n moves
**Loop inside loop** (both to n) → n × n moves
**Halving** (ignore half each step) → about log₂ n moves — tiny! (1024 items ≈ 10 halvings)
**Lucky vs unlucky day**: same program can finish early (found at first spot) or late (last spot). We plan for the UNLUCKY day — it's what users remember.

blocks.label: count the passes yourself

blocks.title: Trace: linear search for 9 in {7,3,9,1}
steps: if 9 were missing: all 4 checks wasted

blocks.md: **The habit you're building:** before coding, say the pass count out loud: *"this will be one pass"* or *"pairs, so heavy"*. That sentence IS complexity thinking.

items.q: A loop halves a pile of 1024 cards until one remains. How many rounds?
Why plan for the unlucky day?
options: users hit the worst case eventually; it defines reliability
items.explain: Worst-case promises are what interviews and real systems run on.

sections.title: Your toolbox — containers that do the work for you

blocks.md: **The STL is a shelf of ready-made machines. Each has a talent — pick the machine whose talent matches your job.**

items: **vector** — a stretchable row; instant access by position `v[i]`; attach at end cheaply
**set** — auto-sorted unique items; asks *"do you contain x?"* quickly without scanning everything
**map<Key,Value>** — a dictionary: look up meaning by word, not by page number
**stack / queue** — one-door line (last in first out) / two-door line (first in first out)
**priority_queue** — hands you the BIGGEST item instantly, every time

blocks.label: three machines in action
blocks.py:
v = [5, 2, 8]
v.append(1)                 # row grows
v.sort()                    # [1,2,5,8]

s = {5, 2, 8, 2}            # set refuses duplicates -> {2,5,8}
have8 = 8 in s              # fast membership ask

age = {'Asha': 21, 'Bilal': 22}   # dictionary = key->value map
print(age['Asha'])

blocks.md: **Talent table (memorize the feelings):** vector = positional access · set/map = ordered questions · priority_queue = biggest-first · stack/queue = order-keeping machines.

items.q: Need to check 'have I seen this number before?' millions of times — which machine?
items.explain: Scanning costs a full pass per question; set answers without walking the whole shelf.

items.q: Need the LARGEST score repeatedly from a changing pile?
items.explain: It exists precisely to serve biggest-first requests instantly.

items.q: After sort(v.begin(), v.end()) on {5,2,8}, v[0] holds…
items.explain: Smallest first under default ascending sort.

sections.title: Seeing growth with your own eyes

blocks.md: Notice: pairs-style dies between 10⁴ and 10⁶ inputs while scans stay comfortable. When constraints say n is big, pairs-style is banned before you even start typing.
**Big input kills nested loops first. Check input size, then choose your loop shape.**

sections.title: Problem set — L1 drills (one counting skill each)

items.title: Max in Array (one scan)
items.statement: Find the largest element with exactly one walk through the array.
hints: Carry the champion so far; challenge it with each new element.
Start champion = a[0], loop from i=1.

solutionCode.label: carry the champion

items.complexity: One pass: n − 1 comparisons. Space O(1).

followups.q: Why start the champion at a[0] rather than 0?
followups.a: Seeding with 0 assumes the array contains a positive number. On all-negative input like [-5,-2,-9] it would wrongly return 0, a value that is not even in the array. Seeding with a real element can never do that.

followups.q: How many comparisons for n = 1,000,000?
followups.a: Exactly 999,999 — one per element after the first. There is no way to do better: any element you never compare could have been the maximum, so n − 1 is a proven lower bound.

items.title: Second Max (still one scan)
items.statement: Largest AND second largest in a single pass — no sorting allowed.
hints: Keep two champions: best, runnerUp.
New king demotes old king to runner-up.
Careful with duplicates: equal doesn't dethrone twice.

solutionCode.label: two champions, demote on a new king

items.complexity: One pass, at most 2 comparisons per element. Space O(1).

followups.q: What should [5, 5, 3] return, and why is that a design decision?
followups.a: This code returns (5, 3): the `x < best` guard means a duplicate of the maximum cannot also be the second maximum. That is the "distinct second largest" reading. If duplicates should count, drop that guard and you get (5, 5). Ask which one the problem wants before coding — both are defensible.

followups.q: Why not sort and take the last two?
followups.a: Sorting costs n log n to obtain information a single pass already gives in n − 1 comparisons. On a million elements that is roughly 20 million operations instead of 1 million.

items.title: Sum & Count of Evens
items.statement: In one pass, output both the count of even numbers and their sum.
hints: a % 2 == 0 test.
Two accumulators update together.

solutionCode.label: two accumulators updated together

followups.q: Does `x % 2 == 0` work for negative numbers?
followups.a: Yes. In both C++ and Python, −4 % 2 is 0, so even negatives are detected. Testing `x % 2 == 1` for oddness is the one that breaks: in C++ −3 % 2 is −1, not 1. Use `x % 2 != 0` for odd.

followups.q: Why is the sum a 64-bit type?
followups.a: A million elements near 10^9 sum to 10^15, which overflows a 32-bit int at around 2×10^9. The count is safe, but the sum is not — mismatched accumulator widths are a common silent bug.

items.title: Linear Search + Position
items.statement: Return index of target or −1. Then predict: worst-day checks for n=1,000,000?
hints: Early return on match.
Missing target walks everything — that's the worst day.

solutionCode.label: early return on match

items.complexity: Best case 1 comparison, worst case n. Space O(1).

followups.q: Worst-day checks for n = 1,000,000?
followups.a: One million. The worst case is the target being absent, or sitting in the last position — both force the full walk. The average for a present target is about n/2, but the worst case is what you quote.

followups.q: When is linear search the right choice despite being O(n)?
followups.a: When the data is unsorted and you search it once — sorting first costs n log n, which is worse than a single n scan. It also wins on tiny arrays where cache locality beats the branching of binary search.

items.title: Is Sorted?
items.statement: Check ascending order comparing NEIGHBORS only.
hints: Compare a[i] <= a[i+1] across one pass.
First violation → immediate false.

solutionCode.label: compare neighbours only

items.complexity: Worst case n − 1 comparisons, early exit on the first violation. Space O(1).

followups.q: Why is comparing only neighbours enough?
followups.a: Ordering is transitive: if every adjacent pair is in order, then a[i] ≤ a[i+1] ≤ … ≤ a[j] for any i < j. Checking all pairs would be n² comparisons for information the n − 1 adjacent ones already imply.

followups.q: Should an empty array be "sorted"?
followups.a: By convention yes — the condition "every adjacent pair is ordered" is vacuously true when there are no pairs. The loop returns true naturally, but say it out loud, because some interviewers want an explicit guard.

items.title: Reverse In Place
items.statement: Reverse an array WITHOUT a second array.
hints: Swap ends walking inward.
Stop when pointers cross.

solutionCode.label: swap the ends, walk inward

items.complexity: n/2 swaps, one pass. Space O(1).

followups.q: What happens if the loop uses `l <= r`?
followups.a: When l == r the element swaps with itself — harmless but wasted work. The real bug is writing `l != r` on an even-length array: the pointers cross without ever being equal and the loop runs off both ends. `l < r` is safe for both parities.

followups.q: How many swaps for n = 7?
followups.a: Three. Pairs (0,6), (1,5), (2,4) swap; index 3 is the midpoint and stays put. In general floor(n/2), which is why an odd-length array leaves its centre untouched.

items.title: Pair Count Discovery
items.statement: Count unordered pairs (i<j) with nested loops; verify result equals n*(n-1)/2 for n=5.
hints: Inner loop starts at j=i+1 (no self-pairs, no double-count).
Formula check connects loops to math.

solutionCode.label: inner loop starts at i+1

items.complexity: Nested loops run n(n−1)/2 times — quadratic growth. Space O(1).

followups.q: Verify the formula for n = 5.
followups.a: The loop runs 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 10 times. The formula gives 5×4/2 = 10. They match, which is the point: the nested loop *is* the sum 1 + 2 + … + (n−1), and that sum has the closed form n(n−1)/2.

followups.q: What does that mean for n = 100,000?
followups.a: About 5×10^9 iterations — minutes, not milliseconds. This is the concrete reason "nested loop over the same array" is a red flag at scale, and why the next exercise replaces it with a set.

items.title: Seen-Before Checker
items.statement: First duplicate finder: naive nested version, then re-implement with a set. Feel the speed difference on n=100,000.
hints: Naive: for each i scan j<i — pairs territory!
Set version: ask set before inserting; first YES is the answer.

solutionCode.label: naive pairs vs ask-the-set

items.complexity: Naive: up to n(n−1)/2 comparisons. Set version: O(n) average, one pass. Space O(1) vs O(n).

followups.q: Quantify the difference at n = 100,000.
followups.a: Naive is ~5×10^9 comparisons — tens of seconds at best. The set version is 100,000 hash operations, effectively instant. Same answer, four orders of magnitude apart, which is what "feel the difference" means here.

followups.q: What did the speed cost you?
followups.a: O(n) memory for the set, and reliance on hashing being O(1) average — adversarial inputs can degrade it. The naive version uses no extra memory at all. Speed for space is the trade you just made; name it rather than assuming faster is always better.

items.title: Top-K Biggest via priority_queue
items.statement: From n numbers, print the k largest using priority_queue only (k << n).
hints: Push everything, pop k times.
Each pop serves current biggest — no full sort needed.

solutionCode.label: max-heap, pop k times
solutionCode.py:
import heapq


def top_k(a: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
    # Python's heapq is a MIN-heap, so negate to emulate a max-heap
    pq = [-x for x in a]
    heapq.heapify(pq)                 # O(n), not O(n log n)
    out = []
    for _ in range(min(k, len(pq))):
        out.append(-heapq.heappop(pq))   # current biggest
    return out

items.complexity: Build O(n), then k pops at O(log n) each: O(n + k log n). Space O(n).

followups.q: Why is this better than sorting when k is small?
followups.a: Sorting costs n log n to order all n elements when you only need k of them. Heapify is O(n) and each pop is O(log n), so you pay O(n + k log n). For k = 10 out of a million, that is roughly n instead of 20n.

followups.q: There is an even better approach for small k — what is it?
followups.a: Keep a size-k MIN-heap instead: push each element, and pop whenever the heap exceeds k. That is O(n log k) time and, crucially, O(k) space rather than O(n) — it never holds the whole dataset, so it works on a stream.

items.title: Word Frequency Dictionary
items.statement: Count occurrences of each word using map<string,int>; print words alphabetically (free!).
hints: freq[word]++ creates-or-increments.
map prints sorted by key automatically.

solutionCode.label: map<string,int> counts and sorts at once

items.complexity: O(n log n) total with std::map (log n per insert); iteration is already in sorted order for free.

followups.q: What does `++freq[w]` do when the word is new?
followups.a: operator[] on a std::map default-constructs the value — 0 for int — and returns a reference to it, which is then incremented to 1. Convenient, but it means merely *reading* `freq[w]` inserts the key. Use `.count()` or `.find()` when you only want to look.

followups.q: When would you use unordered_map instead?
followups.a: When you do not need sorted output. unordered_map gives O(1) average insert versus O(log n), so it is faster to build — but you would then have to sort the results yourself, which costs the saving back if sorted output is the requirement.
